object_entity.description: Baptism is not merely symbolic but effects a new birth or regeneration of the recipient.

evidence.notes: Baptism as seal; descend and come up alive

passage.excerpt: These apostles and teachers preached the name of the Son of God to those who had fallen asleep before them, and they also gave them the seal of the preaching. They descended therefore into the water with them and again came up. But these went down alive and came up alive; but those who had previously fallen asleep went down dead but came up alive. Through them they were made alive and came to know the name of the Son of God.
passage.notes: Baptism as seal necessary for salvation; retroactive sealing of the dead

object_entity.description: Fasting is a required Christian spiritual discipline presented as obligatory, not merely optional.

evidence.notes: Hermas Similitude 5 discusses proper fasting extensively.

passage.excerpt: As I was fasting and sitting on a certain mountain, giving thanks to the Lord for all that He had done to me, I see the Shepherd sitting beside me. He said to me: Why have you come here so early? I said: Because, sir, I am keeping a station. What is a station? he asked. I am fasting, sir, I said. What is this fast that you are keeping? he asked. I fast as I have been accustomed, sir, I said. You do not know how to fast to the Lord, he said; this useless fast that you keep for Him is no fast.
passage.notes: Hermas discusses proper fasting; the Shepherd corrects mere ritual fasting; true fasting is moral obedience

object_entity.notes: Dispute c. 190-195 between Victor of Rome and Asian churches led by Polycrates of Ephesus over whether Easter should be observed on 14 Nisan or the Sunday following; Irenaeus of Lyons mediated and persuaded Victor not to excommunicate the Asian churches.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Irenaeus wrote to Victor of Rome urging peace over the Easter controversy; he noted that diverse custom on this point does not destroy the unity of the faith, citing Polycarp's visit to Anicetus as a precedent for peaceful disagreement; the difference in fasting does not harm the faith.
passage.notes: Irenaeus mediates Quartodeciman controversy; cites Polycarp's visit to Rome as precedent; peace over uniformity
